exp.1:8:
She says her beloved is like a roe or a young hart: swift, quick and graceful animals. Now he stands behind the wall of the house, looking in through the windows and showing himself through the lattice. "Behold him here" means "look, there he is."

The beloved is the young woman in love, the female voice in the Song of Songs. She has just heard her lover coming, leaping over the mountains, and she describes him with joy. He is close, but there is still a wall between them. Many see here only a poem about married love; others also see an image of God's love for his people, though that is debated.

For today: value and cherish the love of those who are near you. And if you read this text thinking of Christ, remember that he draws near with tenderness; open your "window" and answer him with confidence.
exp.3:5:
It says that, until morning comes and the shadows of night are gone, the speaker will go to the "mountain of myrrh" and the "hill of frankincense." The phrase "break of day" means that the day begins to dawn. "I will get me" means "I will go." Myrrh and frankincense were very prized perfumes.

Here the bridegroom speaks to his beloved, in a love poem. After praising her beauty, he says he will stay close to her, in that place of fragrance. Many understand the mountains as a poetic image of the beloved; others think they are real places or an expression of intimacy. The text does not fully clarify this. Next he tells her that she is beautiful and without blemish.

For today: in love and in life, it is not enough to say pretty words. We can choose to stay, to care for and value those we love, even in dark times, until the light comes.
exp.0:11:
It says that while the king was seated at the table or reclining on his couch, the fragrance of the young woman's perfume spread through the room. The place where one lies down to eat, perhaps at a banquet, is what the earlier wording refers to by a word not used in the verse above, so that description is rendered here as "the couch where he reclined." The perfume itself is a very expensive aromatic oil brought from far away. Saying that her fragrance "gave off its scent" means that its aroma was noticed.

The speaker is the young wife, the beloved of the Song of Songs. After hearing others praise him, she answers with tenderness toward her beloved, whom she calls "king." Some see here poetic language of love between spouses; others also read it as an image of the love between God and his people. Interpreters do not agree on every detail.

For today: true love is expressed through sincere and carefully given gifts. We can offer God and those we love the best of our time, attention, and affection, like a perfume that brightens the atmosphere.
exp.6:9:
She says she belongs to her beloved, and that he desires her with affection. "Delight" is an old-fashioned word meaning pleasure, enjoyment, or delight; in other versions this line is rendered "his desire is toward me."

In this poem, the speaker is the woman, the Shulammite. Until now her beloved has praised her beauty, and she answers with confidence and joy. Compare 2:16 and 6:3, where she says something similar. Here the tone shifts a little: she no longer only says "he is mine," but recognizes herself as his, and right away she invites him to go out into the countryside. Many see here a picture of married love; some also read it as an image of God's love for his people, though this is understood in different ways.

For today: in marriage, healthy love is lived out with mutual commitment and without fear. Today you can tell your partner how much you value them, with words and concrete gestures. And if you are single, remember that your worth does not depend on anyone else.
exp.3:15:
The explanation says that the north wind (Aquilon) and the south wind (Austro) should blow upon the garden so that the fragrance of its plants is spread abroad. Then the speaker invites her beloved to enter her garden and eat of its sweet fruit. The phrase "let the spices flow out" means that the scents are to be released and carried everywhere.

In the Song of Songs, the garden is a poetic image of the bride, described in the preceding verses as a locked garden full of spices. Here she speaks and gives herself freely to her beloved. Many see in this the love of marriage; others, since ancient times, have also read it as an image of the love between God and his people. Both readings have been upheld.

For today: offer what God has given you, your time, your gifts and your affection, freely and generously. And in your marriage, or in your relationship with God, cultivate a love that gives itself with trust and not with calculation.
exp.0:0:
It says this is the best of the songs, "the song of songs," a Hebrew way of expressing what is most excellent, as in "king of kings." It also says it is "of Solomon," which may mean that he wrote it, that it was written for him, or that it is about him. Scholars understand this in different ways.

It is the opening verse of the book, so no speaker has yet appeared. It works as a title that introduces a love poem between a husband and a wife, and the voices begin in the following verse. Many Jews and Christians have seen in it a teaching about human love, and others have also seen a reflection of God's love for his people.

For today: value love and marriage as a gift from God, worthy of being cared for with tenderness, faithfulness, and words that encourage the other person.
exp.0:8:
It says the beloved compares his beloved to a mare among Pharaoh's chariot horses. The first quoted word, "Yegua," is the female horse, and the second, "amiga mía," is an expression of affection. It is a compliment, though it may sound strange today.

The man speaks in reply to the young woman who asked him where he pastures his flock. Many understand the image as pointing to the beauty, strength and elegance of Egyptian horses, which were highly valued and richly adorned. Some believe it also speaks of how imposing she is to him. Scholars do not fully agree on the exact nuance of the comparison. The next verse mentions adornments, which fits the idea of beauty.

Today we can learn to express sincere and specific appreciation to those we love, with careful words suited to their character. A genuine compliment strengthens a relationship, and it also reminds us that God values the beauty of pure and faithful love.
exp.6:5:
It says the beloved is very beautiful and pleasing. Sweet, tender, and delightful are the sense of the first phrase. The second phrase means love that brings great joy and happiness. It is an exclamation of admiration, like when someone is left speechless before a cherished person.

The one speaking is the husband, who, after describing his beloved with poetic images from the ancient world (towers, pools, mountains), sums it all up with this simple praise. Not all scholars agree on every detail of the poem, but many see it as a song about married love. Some also read it as a picture of God's love for his people, though this is interpreted in several ways.

Today we can learn to express appreciation for those we love, especially in marriage, with sincere and kind words. A true and timely compliment strengthens affection, and it reminds us that faithful love is a gift from God to be enjoyed with gratitude.
exp.6:4:
It says that the beloved's head stands with dignity, like Mount Carmel, a green mountain range by the sea. Her bright, dark hair is compared to the king's purple, a very costly cloth.

Here the husband speaks, in a poem that praises his wife's beauty with images of places and objects from his land. These are poetic comparisons, not literal descriptions. He wants to express admiration, wonder, and a love that sees her as someone precious, almost royal.

For today: in marriage, sincere words of appreciation build up. Praising with tenderness and respect the person you love strengthens the bond. Today you can tell someone close to you something specific that you admire in that person.
exp.2:8:
This verse says that King Solomon had a chariot made for himself, or a litter to carry him, from wood of Lebanon. That wood, which came from the famous cedars, was highly valued for its quality and its fragrance. The word "chariot" here does not mean a wheeled carriage but a portable seat, like a royal chair that was carried.

It is part of a wedding poem. The speaker seems to be the voice of the bride or a narrator describing a royal procession, with guards who protect the king. Scholars debate whether the scene is a royal wedding, a memory, or a poetic image of love. The text does not fully make this clear.

For today: just as here someone is cared for and honored with devotion because they are loved, we can give our best, our time and attention, to the important relationships in our lives, and to God first.
exp.1:3:
It says that the beloved brought his beloved into the "banqueting house," which in the Hebrew is literally "house of wine" and was probably a place for a feast or celebration. The "banner" that waved over her was love: a sign that she belonged to him and was under his care.

The young bride of the poem speaks here, joyfully recalling how her beloved receives and honors her. Shortly before, she compared him to a sweet apple tree and rested in his shade. Some understand the "wine" as an image of joy and marital intimacy; others see here a royal banquet. The text does not make clear what the exact place is.

For today: true love shows itself openly and gives security. If you are married, honor your spouse with clear words and gestures. And all of us can remember that God's love also covers our life like a protective banner.
exp.5:9:
This verse asks a question full of wonder: who is this woman who appears like the dawn, beautiful as the moon, bright as the sun? The word "clear" describes her as luminous and radiant. The phrase "awe-inspiring like an army in formation" speaks of a beauty that impresses and commands respect, like an army with its banners in order.

The ones speaking are the young women, the queens, and the concubines from the previous verse, who watch the beloved pass by and praise her. Earlier, the lover called her "my dove, my perfect one," unique among many. Some understand this as an exaltation of the bride; others see it as an image of faithful and exclusive love.

For today: faithful and sincere love has a value that impresses more than appearance or fame. Keep your commitments with steadiness, and praise generously the one you love.
exp.4:3:
What it says: The woman tells how her beloved tried to open the door by putting his hand through the opening in it. When she sensed him so near, her inner being was stirred with emotion and tenderness. Today we would say her heart skipped a beat.

Context: The speaker is the beloved, the young woman of the Song of Songs. She remembers a night when she was half asleep and her beloved knocked at the door. She hesitated with excuses: she was already ready for bed. Her emotion made her get up, but he had already gone. Some see here only a story of human love; others see an image of the love between God and his people.

For today: When you sense God calling you to your heart, do not put it off for comfort or tiredness. Respond promptly, even with a simple prayer, because moments of closeness are precious.
exp.2:6:
It says that Solomon's litter, a kind of covered couch or chair that was carried to transport an important person, is surrounded by sixty valiant men. They are among the strongest soldiers of Israel, and their task is to protect the king and whoever travels with him.

This is in the Song of Songs, a love poem. It is probably spoken by the voice of the young women or of the narrator, describing a wedding procession. Some think the litter carries the king, others that it carries the bride. Scholars do not fully agree. What is clear is that the verse emphasizes the security and honor of love.

For today: true love deserves care and protection. Look after your marriage, your courtship, or your friendships with prayer, wisdom, and healthy boundaries. We can also remember that God cares for his own with greater strength than any guard.
exp.0:13:
Here the bride says that her beloved is like a cluster of henna blossoms in the vineyards of En-gedi. Henna is a fragrant plant with flowers that grow in clusters, and it is the word the King James Version calls "camphire." En-gedi was a fertile oasis beside the Dead Sea, a green and fragrant place in the middle of dry ground.

The one speaking is the young woman in love. She has just compared her beloved to myrrh, another precious perfume. Now she uses another image from the world of fragrance and nature to express how much she values him. For her, he is a rare gift, sweet and refreshing.

For today: learn to name with affection what is valuable in the people you love. A sincere compliment, spoken at the right time, can be a perfume that brings joy to the heart of your spouse, a friend, or your family.
exp.6:8:
The explanation says that the beloved's words and kisses are like good wine: they glide down smoothly and even make the lips of the elderly speak. Here "roof of the mouth" refers to the mouth, the kiss, and the voice. The phrase that goes down smoothly means it slides along easily, and some translations say "lips of those that are asleep," because the original is hard to translate.

The book is a love poem between a husband and his wife. In this section the husband praises his beloved, and she seems to break in to complete the image with joy. Then she says: "I am my beloved's." It is a love that rejoices and gives itself freely.

For today: the Bible presents married love as a good gift from God. Practice it with tender and sincere words toward your spouse or toward those you love. A kind word spoken at the right moment can bring encouragement and joy.
exp.1:2:
She says her beloved stands out among the young men, just as an apple tree stands out among the trees of the forest, which bear no fruit. "Young men" is the meaning of the word for the sons in the verse. The "beloved" is the one she desires, the one she longs for. She sat down in his shadow, that is, she found rest and protection, and his fruit was sweet to her, that is, it gave her joy and delight.

Here the beloved woman, the bride, is speaking, answering the praise he has just given her when he compared her to a lily among thorns. She returns the compliment with another image from nature. It is a poem of love between husband and wife. Some believers also read it as an image of God's love for his people, though not all agree on this.

For today: let us learn to say out loud the good we see in the people we love. Today, thank someone close to you with sincere and specific words.
exp.0:2:
It says the beloved has a pleasant aroma, because of his fine perfumes. His name is like poured-out perfume, that is, the mere mention of it spreads and delights. That is why the young women love him. "Ointments" are scented oils, and "virgins" are unmarried young women.

Here the beloved woman, the young woman of the poem, speaks to her lover, who is called the king. She has just said that his love is better than wine. Now she speaks of his fame and his character, not only of his attractiveness. Some see here a song of marital love; others, since ancient times, also see an image of the love between God and his people. Both readings have been upheld.

For today: take care of your name, your reputation and your character. Living with kindness and faithfulness leaves a good fragrance on others, and it also strengthens love in marriage and in friendships.
exp.3:4:
It says the beloved's breasts are like two young twin gazelle fawns that graze quietly among lilies. It is poetic language that speaks of tenderness, beauty, delicacy and life. The lilies suggest something fresh and lovely, and the twins speak of harmony and balance.

Here the bridegroom speaks, admiringly describing his beloved in a love song. He is in the middle of a long praise that moves over her face, her neck and her figure. Shortly after, he calls her "all beautiful," without blemish. Some see only marital love; others also see an image of God's love for his people. Both readings have been held throughout history.

For today: love in marriage is nurtured with sincere, respectful words full of appreciation. Today you can praise your spouse with tenderness and purity, without mockery or unkind comparisons.
exp.1:7:
She says that the beloved woman recognizes her lover's voice before she sees him. She pictures him coming with great energy and joy, leaping over the mountains and bounding across the hills. Nothing stops him; no obstacle is too great for him to reach her.

She is the young woman speaking in the Song of Songs, a love poem between her and her beloved. This comes after her longing to be near him and her request that the daughters of Jerusalem not stir up love before its time. Here her heart fills with emotion as she anticipates his arrival. Some see only human love; others also see a reflection of God's love for his people. Both readings are possible.

For today: learn to recognize and value the voice of the one who truly loves you. In marriage, friendship, and faith, listening carefully and responding with joy strengthens love. God also speaks to us with tenderness; set aside time to hear him.
exp.5:3:
It says the beloved is beautiful like Tirzah and desirable like Jerusalem. "My love" is a tender form of address. Tirzah was a city known for its beauty and later became the capital of the northern kingdom. "Terrible as an army with banners" (other versions say "majestic as an army with its banners") speaks of a beauty that impresses and leaves one speechless.

Here the lover speaks and praises his beloved. It comes right after she declares: "I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine." He responds with admiration. Interpreters see in the book a poem of married love, and some also read it as a picture of God's love for his people. This last point is interpreted in several ways.

For today: do not keep sincere praise to yourself. Today, tell your spouse or someone dear to you what you admire in that person, using clear and affectionate words.
exp.0:7:
It says that, if she does not know where to find her beloved, she should go out following the footsteps of the flock. She should take her young goats to graze near the "cabañas," that is, the huts or tents of the shepherds. She is called "the fairest among women" with affection.

The young woman has just asked where her beloved rests at midday. Here the voice of the beloved answers, although some think it is the women of Jerusalem; the text does not clarify this completely. It has a tender and somewhat playful tone. He tells her to look for him along the simple path, where the shepherds are. Then he praises her in the following verse.

For today: if you want to find Christ, look where He usually is: in His Word, in prayer, and in fellowship with His people. Steadily follow the footsteps of those who have walked faithfully with Him, and keep doing your daily tasks while you seek Him.
exp.0:15:
Here the bride answers the words of her beloved. He told her she is beautiful, and now she returns the praise: "You are handsome, my beloved, and pleasant", that is, agreeable and sweet. "Bed" is the couch where they rest, and "flowering" means full of blossoms, fresh and green. She speaks of a place of rest and closeness, surrounded by natural beauty.

The one speaking is the woman of the poem, the Shulammite. Song of Songs is a love song between two spouses, and here both admire each other with tenderness. Interpreters read it in different ways: as a praise of married love, or also as an image of God's love for his people. The Bible does not require us to choose just one.

For today: learn to praise sincerely the person you love. Kind and grateful words can strengthen a marriage, a friendship or a family.
exp.4:12:
He says that the beloved's cheeks are like a bed of fragrant plants, like scented flowers. His lips are like lilies that drip myrrh, a costly perfume that spreads and is noticed far beyond where it is applied. Here the garden picture is a plot of ground being cultivated.

The wife is speaking. The daughters of Jerusalem asked her what makes her beloved special, and she answers by describing him from head to foot with images of richness and beauty. Many read it as poetry of marital love. Others also see a picture of the love between God and his people; both readings are possible.

For today: learn to speak well of the people you love, with concrete and grateful words. Lips that drip with myrrh bless rather than wound. Today, tell someone close to you something specific that you value in them.
exp.3:13:
This verse continues listing the plants of the garden: spikenard, saffron, calamus, cinnamon, frankincense trees, myrrh, aloes, and the finest spices. The calamus is a fragrant reed used for perfume, and the aloes mentioned here is a fragrant wood, not the medicinal plant. These are fine, costly scents, brought from distant lands.

Here the bridegroom speaks, praising his beloved with the image of a closed garden filled with perfumes. That image expresses that she is precious, unique, and reserved for him. Many see here poetry of marital love; some also read it as a reflection of God's love for his people, although opinions vary.

For today: value and care for what God has entrusted to you, above all your marriage or your other important relationships. Tell that person words of sincere appreciation, because affection spoken tenderly is like a good perfume.
exp.4:8:
Here, some women ask the young woman: "What is your beloved more than another beloved?" They call her "the fairest among women" and ask her to explain why she begs them so urgently. "Charge" means to urge insistently, almost as if under an oath.

The speakers are the "daughters of Jerusalem," a group of young women. The young woman has just asked them that, if they find her beloved, they tell him she is sick with love. Their question gives her the opening to describe him in the verses that follow. Many read it as poetry about married love. Others also see an image of the love between God and his people, though there are different interpretations.

For today: when someone asks you why you love Christ, or the people God has placed in your life, do not give a vague answer. Think about, and practice, how to explain simply what makes them valuable to you.
exp.5:5:
Her teeth are like a flock of sheep that have just come up from the washing, each one bearing twins, and none of them has lost its young. That is, her teeth are complete, even, and in perfect order. The place where the sheep were bathed is the washing place, and the young ones are the pair born together.

Here the husband speaks, still praising his beloved with images from the countryside. This verse nearly repeats what he said earlier in Song of Songs 4:2. Many understand that the poem celebrates married love. Some also read it as a reflection of God's love for his people, although interpreters do not agree on this point.

For today: learn to express your appreciation with concrete and sincere words. If you are married, or have someone you love, notice the good in that person and tell them so. A kind and specific word strengthens affection and trust.
exp.1:6:
Here the young bride asks the daughters of Jerusalem not to stir up love before its time. She asks this with great seriousness, almost as if swearing an oath. The roes and the hinds are delicate creatures of the field, and through them she gives strength to her request. In this verse, to stir up means to awaken or disturb. Until it pleases means until love itself is ready.

She is speaking in the Song of Songs, after describing her desire and the nearness of her beloved. The daughters of Jerusalem are the women who listen to her. She does not reject love; she values it so highly that she asks for its moment to be respected. Some understand that love should not be forced; others, that it should not be awakened outside of marriage.

Today we can care for love with patience: not rushing relationships or emotions, but waiting for the right time and asking God for wisdom.
exp.1:5:
She says she wishes her beloved would hold her gently: that his left arm would serve as a pillow under her head, and that his right arm would embrace her. It is an image of closeness, affection, and security.

The one speaking is the beloved young woman of the Song of Songs, who feels overwhelmed by love, that is, overcome by the emotion of his affection. Some read the book as a poem about married love; others also see in it a picture of God's love for his people. Shortly before, she speaks of being brought into the wine house, and then she asks the daughters of Jerusalem not to stir up love before its time.

For today: value love and care for it with patience, without rushing it. May there be tenderness in marriage, and in other relationships may we wait for the right moment.
exp.1:16:
The explanation says that the beloved asks her lover to come back to her until morning arrives, when the day breaks and the shadows flee away, that is, when the night is over. "Turn" means "come back." She compares him to a gazelle (a deer) or a young stag, animals that are agile and swift. "Bether" is an uncertain name: some take it as a real place, others as "the mountains of division" or "of separation."

The young wife speaks in this love poem. She has just said that she and her beloved belong to each other. Now she invites him to stay close and to return soon. Interpreters differ: some see here only the longing of lovers; others see an image of the love between God and his people.

For today: take care of love and closeness in your relationships, above all in marriage. Make time to be present, to express affection, and to seek God with that same longing, especially in difficult nights, trusting that morning comes.
exp.7:3:
It says that the beloved speaks to the young women of Jerusalem and asks them earnestly, almost like an oath, not to stir up or awaken love until he himself is ready. The word "charge" in the verse above means that she is urging them with solemn seriousness. The phrase "stir not up" refers to not provoking or agitating love. In other words, love should not be forced or hurried.

The bride speaks in this love poem. She has just expressed her desire to be close to her beloved, with a tender embrace. This same plea also appears in Song of Solomon 2:7 and 3:5, as a kind of refrain. Many understand it as a call to wait for the right moment; others see it as advice not to awaken passions before their time. Both readings fit the context.

For today: do not force relationships or let others pressure you. Let love grow with patience, sincerity, and respect, trusting that God knows the times.
exp.2:9:
This verse describes in detail the carriage of King Solomon. Its pillars were silver, its backrest gold, and its roof or covering was crimson, a deep red fabric. The phrase "paved with love" is difficult: the Hebrew is uncertain. Some think the inside was decorated with inlays made with care, and others that it was a gift of love from the young women of Jerusalem.

The poetic voice of the book speaks, presenting a wedding procession. The riches, the safety (the warriors of the previous verse), and the affection with which everything was prepared stand out. Scholars debate whether this is a real scene, a symbolic one, or an imagined one.

For today: true love is shown in care and in attention to details. Ask yourself how you can prepare a place of warmth and security for your family, your partner, or your community, serving with tenderness rather than with appearances.
exp.3:12:
The explanation says that what springs from the beloved is like an orchard of pomegranates, with delicious fruits, and with fragrant plants such as henna and spikenard. The word "shoots" refers to the young growths or sprouts of a garden. "Enclosed garden" here means a walled orchard or garden, not heaven. The old term for henna, a shrub with fragrant flowers, is the word used in the verse (some interpret it as camphor, but this is not certain).

The speaker is the husband, the beloved, who praises his wife with the image of an exquisite garden, enclosed and reserved only for him. It is love poetry; it uses figurative language to express admiration, beauty and exclusivity in marriage.

For today: learn to value and express, in kind words, the good you see in the people you love, above all in your spouse. And faithfully care for that bond, like someone who tends a garden that deserves attention and protection.
exp.7:6:
The explanation says that true love is so strong that nothing can put it out. The "many waters" and the "floods" stand for the trials, problems, and pressures that could destroy it. "Substance" means riches or possessions. "Contemned" means despised or held in low regard. In other words, love cannot be bought: if someone offered all the wealth of their house in exchange for love, people would reject it with scorn.

These words are part of the end of the Song of Songs. The speaker is the young woman, who has just asked her beloved to take her as a seal upon his heart. She explains why: this love is strong as death and burns like fire. Some read it as love between spouses; others also see a reflection of God's love for his people.

For today: love is not sustained by gifts, but by faithfulness and commitment. When the "waters" of life arrive, decide to care for your love with patience, forgiveness, and steadfastness.
exp.4:5:
She says that she opened the door to her beloved, but he was no longer there: he had gone. When she heard his voice, her soul went out after him; that is, she was deeply moved and went to look for him. She searched for him and did not find him; she called him and he did not answer. The bolts are the locks of the door, and myrrh is a perfume.

The young wife of the Song of Songs is speaking. Earlier, her beloved knocked at the door and she was slow to open it. When she finally did, he had already withdrawn. Many see here a poem about human love and its neglect; others also read it as an image of the love between God and his people. Both readings are possible.

For today: do not postpone what is important. If God or someone dear to you seeks you out, respond promptly, and do not let comfort or laziness cool that relationship.
exp.7:12:
Here the beloved speaks to his beloved. He says to her: you who dwell in the gardens, your companions are attentive to your voice, but let me hear it too. "Dwellest" means "dwell," and "cause me to hear it" means "let me hear it."

The book is a love poem between two spouses. After speaking of the vineyard and of her devotion, the beloved asks her to speak to him. She answers in the following verse with an affectionate invitation. Some see here only human love, and others also see a reflection of God's love for his people. Scholars do not fully agree.

For today: in important relationships, listening and speaking with affection is essential. Set aside time to talk unhurriedly with your partner, your family or your friends, and also with God in prayer.
exp.7:10:
Solomon had a vineyard in a place called Baal-hamon. He handed it over to keepers, and each one had to bring him a thousand pieces of silver as the profit from the harvest. The "keepers" are those who look after or manage the vineyard. Neither the exact location of Baal-hamon nor its meaning is known for certain.

Here the beloved young woman speaks, and many understand that she compares Solomon's vineyard with her own. Solomon has great wealth, but she says in the following verse that her own vineyard, that is, herself, is hers and is not for sale. Some think the vineyard symbolizes her person and her love. Others interpret it in a different way.

For today: true love cannot be bought or bargained for with money. Guard your heart and your relationships, and do not give them away for gain or under pressure.
exp.3:0:
Here the bridegroom speaks to his beloved and tells her twice that she is beautiful. He compares her eyes to doves, which suggest tenderness and gentleness, seen through the hair that falls over her face. Her hair, long and dark, looks like a flock of goats coming down in waves from the mountains of Gilead.

The one speaking is the bridegroom, in this love poem between two lovers. It is poetic language full of images from the countryside, not a literal description. Some see here only human love; others also see a reflection of God's love for his people.

For today: do not keep your kind words to yourself. Tell someone you love, today, with sincerity and tenderness, what you value in that person. A sincere compliment can strengthen a relationship a great deal.
exp.0:16:
It says the house of the two of them has beams of cedar, which are the trunks that hold up the roof, and rafters of cypress, which are the roofs or panels of carved wood. These are strong, fragrant and valuable woods. Some translators understand "rafters" as beams or crossbeams; the sense is similar.

The bride speaks in this love poem between two spouses. After the two of them praise each other, she describes the place of their meeting: the flowered bed, under the shade of the trees. Many think it is an open-air refuge, and others a figurative royal house. It is not certain which of the two she imagines, but she expresses that their love feels secure, beautiful and lasting.

For today: take care of your home and your marriage as a firm and welcoming place. With kind words, time together and faithfulness, you can keep building a refuge where love feels protected.
exp.6:0:
Here a man praises his beloved. He says her feet in sandals are beautiful, and he calls her "prince's daughter," meaning a noblewoman. He compares the curve of her hips to jewels made by a skilled craftsman.

It is a poem of love between a husband and wife. The speaker is the beloved, probably Solomon, although some think it is a chorus or a group of friends. He begins his praise with her feet and keeps moving upward in the following verses. The images are ancient and symbolic and should not be read literally.

For today: the Bible presents marital love as a gift from God, worthy of celebration. If you are married, praise your spouse with sincere and respectful words. Valuing your partner as a careful work of God strengthens trust and tenderness.
exp.3:3:
It says the beloved's neck is like the tower of David, built as an impressive work that is displayed with pride. From that tower hang a thousand shields, all belonging to brave warriors. The image speaks of a dignified, firm, and elegant beauty. It is not known with certainty which specific tower is meant.

Here the beloved speaks in the Song of Songs, praising his beloved with poetic, not literal, images. The hanging shields suggest strength and dignity. Many Christians see in the book a celebration of married love; others also read in it a reflection of God's love for his people.

For today: learn to express sincere and specific appreciation to the people you love, especially in marriage. A few well-chosen words can give someone security, encouragement, and courage.
exp.4:9:
He describes the beloved as someone whose beauty sets him apart. "White" probably speaks of a clear, healthy complexion, and "ruddy" of a reddish or rosy color, like good health. "The chiefest among ten thousand" means that he stands out in a huge crowd, so that he can be recognized from a distance. Some scholars understand these words as a physical description, and others as a poetic way of saying that he is incomparable.

The one speaking is the bride. The daughters of Jerusalem asked her what is so special about her beloved, and she answers with this description. She is anguished because she is searching for him and cannot find him, so speaking about him is a way of expressing her love and longing.

For today: when we truly love, we can explain why that person is precious. Let us do the same with God: let us think about what He has done and speak of Him with gratitude and simplicity.
exp.2:2:
The explanation says that the woman, searching for her beloved through the city at night, met the watchmen who were making their rounds. She asked them whether they had seen the one her soul loves, that is, the person she loves most. The words "found me" mean that they came upon her, and "go about" means that they keep watch as they move through the streets.

The speaker is the young woman of the Song of Songs. Earlier, she looked for him in her bed and did not find him, so she got up to search the streets and squares. Many read it as a love poem between spouses; others also see in it an image of God's love for his people. The watchmen do not answer her here, and she goes on until she finds him.

For today: if someone or something very precious has slipped away from you, such as a relationship or your closeness to God, do not stay still. Search with steadiness, ask questions, and seek help from others, without giving up.
exp.7:8:
It says that, depending on what the younger sister is like, her brothers will make a decision. If she is like a wall, that is, firm and able to protect herself, they will honor her by building a palace of silver upon her. If she is like a door, open and vulnerable, they will protect her with boards of cedar, a strong wood. Rewriting the phrase about the wall and the door, the verse itself speaks of building upon her and enclosing her, which is the sense the explanation gives.

The ones speaking seem to be the young woman's brothers, responding to the earlier question about what to do with the younger sister. Some interpreters see here family care and protection; others, a control over her conduct. Her answer in verse 10, "I am a wall," shows that she is already mature and decides for herself.

For today: we can accompany young people with care, encouraging their strength and setting wise limits, without ceasing to trust their growth. Like her, each person can learn to guard their heart with integrity.
exp.1:15:
This verse says that the beloved feels bound to her lover: "My beloved is mine, and I am his." It is a phrase of mutual belonging and trust. The verse's "feedeth" means that he tends or looks after a flock. "Among the lilies" suggests a beautiful, fresh place full of flowers, though some read it as an image of tenderness and delight.

Here the young bride, the beloved of the poem, speaks. She has just heard the invitation of her lover and the mention of the foxes that spoil the blossoming vineyards, which many understand as the small troubles that threaten love. She answers with confidence in her commitment. Some Christians also see in the book an image of God's love for his people, though this is interpreted in different ways.

For today: take care of your important relationships with faithfulness and attention. If you are married, or in a deep friendship, deal in time with the small harms and renew your commitment with words and deeds.
exp.2:10:
This verse invites the young women of Jerusalem (the "daughters of Zion") to go out and look at King Solomon. He wears the crown that his mother placed on him on the day of his wedding, which was also the day of the joy of his heart.

It is part of a love poem. The voice seems to be that of the beloved, or of a narrator, describing with admiration the royal carriage and the king's arrival. Many read it as a wedding scene. It is not known with certainty what crown this was, since the Bible does not say that Solomon's mother placed a crown on him at his wedding. Some understand it as poetic imagery. Others see here a figure of Christ and his church, though that is an interpretation.

For today: learn to celebrate moments of joy with gratitude, above all faithful love. And care for your marriage or your relationships with tenderness and joy.
exp.1:13:
Here the bridegroom speaks with great tenderness to his beloved, calling her "my dove." She is hidden in the clefts of the rock, in high places that are hard to reach. He asks her to let him see her and to let him hear her speak, because he delights in her voice and her face.

The one speaking is the beloved, in a love poem full of springtime imagery. She seems shy or fearful, and he invites her to come out. Many read it simply as a song about marital love; others also read it as a reflection of God's love for his people. Both readings have been held throughout history.

For today: if you hide yourself out of fear, shame, or pain, remember that God invites you to draw near with confidence. Speak to him honestly in prayer, just as you are. And in your close relationships, cultivate a tender way of treating others that helps them feel safe enough to open up.
exp.6:10:
Here the beloved invites her lover to leave the city and go out into the countryside.

The speaker is the wife, the Shulammite. She has just said, "I am my beloved's, and his desire is toward me." Now she takes the initiative and proposes spending time alone, among the vineyards and pomegranate trees, to express their love. Many see here a celebration of married love; others also see a reflection of God's love for his people, though this is understood in different ways.

For today: love is nurtured with quality time. If you are married, find a moment without screens or rush, even if it is a simple walk, to talk and enjoy each other. Even in friendship with God, it does us good to step away for a while.
exp.6:2:
The explanation says that the beloved's breasts are like two young twin fawns of a gazelle. The gazelle is a kind of small deer or antelope. The comparison speaks of tenderness, delicacy, grace and youthful beauty. It is poetic language, not a literal description.

Here the husband, the beloved, speaks and praises his wife with images taken from nature and from the life of his time. Song of Songs celebrates married love, and this poem moves through her body with admiration. Some readers also see a symbolic meaning in God's love for his people, but others read it only as poetry about human love. Both readings have been held throughout history.

For today: God values faithful love within marriage. If you are married, express to your spouse sincere and respectful admiration through kind words. In this way you care for the union and give thanks to God for it.
exp.7:4:
Some voices ask who this woman is, coming up from the wilderness, leaning upon her beloved. She reminds him that she woke him under the apple tree, the same place where she was born, where her mother went through labor pains. "Leaning upon" means resting on someone for support, and "labor pains" refers to the pains of giving birth.

It is a love poem between the bride and her beloved. The question seems to come from those who see them coming, and the answer is hers. Some think the apple tree is a memory of her childhood, and others see it as a symbol of the beginning of love. It is not certain which reading is correct.

Today we can learn that healthy love leans on the other with trust and remembers its origins with gratitude. Think of someone you love and thank them today, with one concrete word, for the road you have traveled together.
exp.7:9:
She says she is like a firm wall, and that her breasts are like towers. With this she expresses that she is now a mature and strong woman. The phrase "then was I in his eyes as one that found favour" means that, in the eyes of her beloved, she is someone who has found peace, or favor and acceptance.

The young wife is speaking, responding to what her brothers said about her "little sister." They doubted whether she was ready for love. She answers that she is, that she kept her purity and now lives in peace with her beloved. Some understand the "wall" as purity and firmness; others see it as strength of character. Interpretations vary.

For today: true security comes from feeling accepted and loved. Guard your integrity and your convictions, and seek relationships where you can rest in peace, without having to pretend.
exp.0:3:
It says the beloved wants to be close to her lover and asks him to keep leading her; she promises to run after him. It tells that the king brought her into his "chambers," that is, into his most private rooms. There will be joy and gladness there. "Remembering your love" means recalling his affection, which she values more than wine. "The upright" are the sincere and just people, who also love him.

The speaker is the young woman in love, the Shulammite, in this love poem. She longs for the closeness of her beloved, whom she calls the king, and her companions, the young women, accompany her. Many read it as marital love; others also see a reflection of God's love for his people. Scholars interpret it in several ways.

For today: cultivate a close relationship with God, seeking his company gladly and not out of obligation. Remembering his love every day brings you more joy than any passing pleasure.
exp.4:0:
Here the bridegroom says that he has come into his garden, which is an image of his beloved. He has already gathered his myrrh and his spices, and he has enjoyed his honey and his wine. "Á" is "a," and "embriagaos" means "enjoy yourselves until you are filled with joy." It is poetic language of love.

The one speaking is the husband, responding to her invitation at the end of the previous chapter. He celebrates the marriage union with images of a garden and a banquet. The words "Eat, friends" may be his words to the guests, or a separate voice blessing the couple; interpreters do not agree. Many also see here a reflection of God's love for his people, although the text deals first with marital love.

For today: value faithful love and cultivate it with tenderness, time, and kind words. If you are married, give your spouse sincere attention. If you are not, learn to honor pure love as a gift from God.
exp.6:1:
It says that the beloved's navel is like a round goblet that never lacks drink, and that her belly is like a heap of wheat set about with lilies. A "goblet" is a cup or vessel; "set about" means surrounded. These are images of beauty, abundance, and joy.

Here the husband speaks, praising his beloved from head to toe, as in a love song. Many understand this poetic language to be mainly intimate and festive. The text does not fully explain every image, and scholars interpret it in various ways, but the general sense is one of admiration and delight.

For today: love in marriage deserves sincere words of appreciation. This week, tell your spouse something specific you admire about him or her, with respect and affection, and remember that God blesses the faithfulness and joy of married couples.
exp.1:11:
It says that spring has arrived. The flowers can now be seen in the fields, the time for singing has come, and in our land the cooing of the turtledove, a bird that returns in that season, can now be heard. The phrase "have appeared" in the verse above refers to the flowers showing themselves, and "the time of singing" is the season for singing and rejoicing.

The beloved speaks, and the young woman recounts what he told her. He invites her to come out because the winter and the rains are now past. Spring is an image of a new season in love. Many believers also see here a reflection of Christ's love for his people, though others read it only as poetry about married love.

After hard seasons, God can open a new stage. Today, ask yourself whether you are staying hidden because of past pain. Accept his invitation to come out, give thanks, and sing again.
exp.1:9:
Here the young woman tells what her beloved said to her. He calls her "my darling" and "my beautiful one," and he invites her: "Rise up... and come away," that is, that she get up and go out with him. The word "darling" expresses affection and closeness.

The speaker is the bride or beloved in the Song of Songs, recalling the visit of her beloved. He arrives in a hurry, like a young deer, and looks in through the window. After saying this, she explains the reason: the winter has passed, the flowers and songs are returning. Many read it as a love poem between people; others also apply it to God's love for his people, although the text does not say this directly.

Today, this voice invites us to come out of whatever keeps us shut in, such as discouragement or routine, and to care with enthusiasm for our most cherished relationships. We can also hear God's affectionate call to draw near to him.
exp.1:10:
It says the winter is already over. The first sentence in the source explains the archaic wording "hase mudado," which is an old way of saying "has changed" or "has gone," so I'll drop that comment and simply state the meaning. The rain has also passed. It announces that a new season has arrived, brighter and full of life.

The one speaking is the beloved, as the young woman tells it in this poem. He invites her to go out with him and enjoy the spring. The book is a love song between a man and a woman. Many read it as a celebration of human love, and others also see a reflection of God's love for his people. Spring symbolizes a new time for love.

For today: if you are going through a cold or difficult season, remember that seasons change. Keep your heart open to the new things God may bring, and dare to take the next step with hope.
exp.5:7:
It says there are sixty queens, eighty concubines (women of the palace with a lower rank than the queens), and countless young women, so many they cannot be counted. It is a way of saying there are beautiful women in abundance.

The one speaking is the lover, who in this poem is traditionally identified with Solomon, though some interpret it differently. After praising his beloved, he compares her with all those women to show that she is unique. In the verses that follow he calls her "my dove, my perfect one," and even the queens praise her.

For today: true love does not compare, and it is not swept away by the crowd of options. Care for and value the person God has placed at your side, and tell them with sincere words that they are unique to you.
exp.7:0:
Here the young woman in love wishes that her beloved were like a brother of hers, someone raised in the same household. "Having nursed at my mother's breasts" is an old-fashioned way of saying "raised by my mother." That way she could find him out in the street, kiss him, and no one would look down on her for it.

The one speaking is the bride in the Song of Songs. In that culture, showing romantic affection in public was not considered proper, but between siblings it was perfectly normal. She wishes to express her love freely and without shame. Scholars understand the book in different ways: as poetry about marital love, or also as an image of God's love for his people.

Today we can learn to value love that is pure, sincere, and respectful, and to make sure our expressions of affection are fitting for the place and the relationship we have.
exp.2:7:
It says that the sixty brave men surrounding Solomon's litter are all armed men trained for battle. Each one carries his sword at his side, hanging from the thigh, ready to be used. The reason is "the fears of the night," that is, the dangers that can appear in the darkness, such as thieves or unexpected attacks. "Expert" means skilled.

The poem of the Song of Songs describes here a wedding or royal procession scene. The speakers are voices within the poem who watch Solomon's litter approach. Some understand it as a literal scene, and others as a poetic image of protected love. The care and courage surrounding the beloved are emphasized. It is not known with certainty who each voice is.

Today we can learn to protect what we love: family, marriage, and faith. We can pray and stay alert to dangers, trusting that God watches over our nights.
exp.0:12:
The young woman says her beloved is to her like a "bundle of myrrh," that is, a small bag of very fragrant resin. "He shall lie all night betwixt my breasts" means that she keeps him very close to her heart, the way one would carry a precious perfume.

The bride speaks in this love poem. She has just mentioned her spikenard, another perfume, and now she describes with tenderness how much she values her beloved and how close she feels to him. Many read it as poetry of married love. Others, since ancient times, also see it as an image of the love between God and his people, though this is an interpretation.

For today: value and cherish closely what you love most. If you are a believer, seek for the presence of Christ to be your treasure held close, not something distant that you remember only now and then.
exp.7:2:
She says she longs to be in the arms of her beloved: his left hand under her head and his right hand embracing her. It is an image of closeness, tenderness, and security. The wish is expressed by the word "esté," which carries the sense of "if only it were so."

The young woman who loves speaks in the Song of Songs. Shortly before, she wished she could show her affection for her beloved without anyone judging her. Here she imagines the intimacy of love within marriage. Then she asks that love not be forced or rushed. Some see here only human love; others also see an image of God's love for his people. Both readings have been held.

For today: value and care for faithful love through simple gestures of affection and presence. And do not rush love; let it grow in its own time, with respect and commitment.
exp.5:2:
It speaks of a total and mutual giving of self between two people who love each other. "I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine" expresses belonging in both directions. The phrase about him feeding among the lilies means that he tends and cares for his beloved, and here it carries the sense of him moving among the lilies, flowers that symbolize beauty and tenderness.

The one speaking is the bride, the Shulammite. The women of Jerusalem asked her where her beloved had gone, and she answers with calm and confidence: she knows where he is, in his garden. After searching for him in anguish, she now rests in the certainty of his love. Many see here only human love; others also see a reflection of the love between God and his people, though this is understood in different ways.

For today: true love is lived with commitment and trust, not only with feelings. If you are married, look today for a concrete way to care for your spouse. And in your faith, remember that you can rest in the knowledge that you belong to God and that he takes care of you.
exp.5:8:
Here the bridegroom says that, although there are many women in the palace, his beloved is unique. He calls his beloved "my dove," a symbol of tenderness and purity. "Undefiled" here speaks of someone whole and without equal to him. "Only one" means the one she is preferred. "Blessed" means happy and favored. "Concubines" were wives of a lower rank. All of them saw her and praised her.

The one speaking is the bridegroom, in this love poem. He compares the sixty queens, the eighty concubines and the maidens without number with his beloved, to show that she has no rival in his heart. Some think it refers to King Solomon, and others see only a poetic device. The text does not fully make this clear.

For today: faithful love is of unique value. If you are married, tell your partner, with words and with actions, that you choose them above anything else. Sincere praise strengthens the bond.
exp.7:5:
She asks her beloved to keep a permanent place in her life. A "seal" and a "mark" were objects that identified their owner and were carried close to the body. She wants to belong to him in a way that is both secure and visible. She declares that love is as strong as death, that no one can escape it. Passion is an ardent and exclusive devotion, and the grave is the tomb. Its flames are like an intense fire.

The one speaking is the young woman of the Song of Songs, addressing her beloved after coming up with him from the wilderness. Many understand this book as a poem about married love. Some also read it as a picture of God's love for his people, and interpreters do not fully agree on this.

For today: true love shows itself in firm and constant commitment. Look after your important relationships with faithfulness, not only with passing feelings.
exp.2:1:
Here the beloved says she will get up and go all over the city, through the streets and the public squares, to look for the one her soul loves. She looked for him, but did not find him.

The words "I will rise now" and "go about the city" in the verse above carry the same sense as the source's opening phrases, so no separate explanation is needed. "In the broad ways" in the verse means the open public spaces where people gathered, which is what the source meant by its word for squares.

The young woman speaks in the Song of Songs, and she continues what she described in the previous verse: she looked for him at night in her bed and did not find him. Many read this as a dream or a longing in the middle of the night. Some see in the book only human love; others also see a reflection of the love between God and his people. Both readings have been held for a long time.

For today: when the one you love feels far away, or even God, do not stay still. Search with steadiness and hope, because in the next verse she finds him.
exp.0:10:
It says someone promises to make the young woman earrings or ornaments of gold, with small details or dots of silver. The word for earrings is one that refers to hanging ornaments worn on the ears. The phrase "studs of silver" is usually understood as pieces or inlays of silver set onto the gold. The Hebrew text is not entirely exact on this detail, so some translate it as "beads" or "studs" of silver.

Here the speakers are "they" (the verb is in the plural: "we will make"). Many think they are the female companions at court, or perhaps the beloved with his companions, responding to the praise in the previous verse. The Bible does not fully clarify this. It is a gesture of affection and honor toward her.

For today: true love shows itself in concrete gestures of appreciation. Today you can honor someone with a kind word, a thoughtful gift, or a sincere acknowledgment. God also adorns us with his grace and values us.
exp.7:1:
She says she wants to bring her beloved to her mother's house, and that there he would teach her. In turn, she would give him to drink spiced wine, sweetened with the juice of her pomegranates. It is poetic language that expresses affection and a desire to give herself joyfully.

The young woman speaking is the beloved in the Song of Songs. Before, she wished he were like a brother, so she could show him affection in public without being criticized. Now she dreams of bringing him into the home, a place of safety and respect. Some think that "you would teach me" refers to her esteem for his wisdom; others see it more as a poetic detail. The text does not fully clarify this.

For today: healthy love seeks honor, openness, and a safe environment. Care for your relationships with respect, and let affection grow in the light, with family and with God, without rushing or shame.
exp.5:11:
Says: "I did not realize; my soul set me like the chariots of Amminadab." The phrase here is among the most difficult in the book. Some understand the name as a proper noun; others read it as "my noble people." The idea seems to be: suddenly I felt carried away, like being in a swift chariot.

The poem depicts lovers, and it is not certain who is speaking: it may be the beloved or the Shulammite. It comes after intense praise of her and after the visit to the garden. It expresses surprise: love carried him further and faster than he expected.

For today: affection can catch us off guard. Let us pause, ask God for wisdom, and care for our relationships with respect, so that love is lived in peace and not in haste.
exp.4:2:
Here the bride says she has already taken off her clothes for the night and has washed her feet. That is why she asks how she can get dressed again and dirty her feet. The phrases "I have put off my coat" and "how shall I put it on?" are rendered directly from the verse itself.

She speaks in the Song of Songs. Her beloved knocks at the door at night and asks her to open it. She is comfortable in her bed and answers with excuses. Many read this as a lapse in love: she hesitates, though afterward she does get up.

Some also read it as a picture of the relationship with God, but the text does not state this directly.

For today: when God speaks to you, or when someone needs your help, do not let comfort become your excuse. Obey promptly, even when it is hard to get up, and ask God for a willing heart.
exp.3:11:
The explanation says the beloved is like a garden enclosed, a spring shut up and sealed. A garden with a fence and a spring with a cover or seal are not open to just anyone. They are a treasure kept back, reserved and of great value. "Sister" here is a term of affection, not a blood relationship.

The speaker is the husband, the beloved, praising his wife in the Song of Songs. He has just praised her beauty, her lips and her fragrance. Many understand that the image speaks of purity and of exclusive devotion to the husband. Others also see a symbol of faithful love between God and his people. Interpreters do not fully agree on this.

For today: care for commitment and faithfulness in your closest relationships. Value what God has given you and protect it with respect, affection and words that build up.
exp.4:10:
Here the bride describes her beloved beginning with his head. She says it is like the finest gold, meaning something very precious, pure, and radiant. His hair is "bushy," that is, full and curling, and "black as a raven," of an intense and glossy black.

The young woman is the speaker of the poem. The women of Jerusalem asked her what makes her beloved special, and she answers with a description full of images. Many understand these to be poetic comparisons rather than a literal portrait. She expresses her admiration and her love.

For today: learn to look at the people you love with appreciation. In marriage or friendship, saying sincere words of value and gratitude strengthens affection. Today, tell someone something specific you admire in that person.
exp.1:0:
She says she is like a simple and beautiful flower. "Rose" is an uncertain translation: the Hebrew word may refer to a wildflower of the field, such as a crocus or a narcissus. "Sharon" was a fertile plain along the coast. The "lily of the valleys" is also a humble flower, not one from a king's garden.

The speaker appears to be the beloved young woman, in this love poem between two lovers. Some believe she says it with modesty, like a common flower; others read it as a cheerful self-confidence. Right after, the beloved replies that she is like a lily among thorns, that is, she stands out among all the others.

For today: learn to receive with humility and gratitude the appreciation of those who love you, and to value others with sincere words. God also sees beauty in what is simple.
exp.3:2:
It says that the beloved's lips are like a thread of deep red (scarlet), and that her way of speaking is lovely. Her temples, that is, the cheeks or the part of the face next to the forehead, are compared to a piece of a split pomegranate, seen behind her locks, which are the strands or the veil of hair. Some think that "temples" refers to the cheeks; the exact meaning is debated.

The speaker is the husband, who praises his beloved with poetic images from his time. He is in a scene of love and admiration, describing her face and body with comparisons drawn from nature. These are not literal measurements, but the language of affection.

For today: kind words build up. Today you could sincerely praise someone you love, whether your spouse, partner, family or friends, and take care that your words are beautiful and bring life.
exp.1:14:
It says that the foxes must be caught, even the little ones, because they damage the vines, which are in blossom, that is, just beginning to flower and still very tender. "Take us" means "catch for us" or "hunt for us." "Spoil" means to ruin or damage.

It is part of a love poem. Interpreters do not agree on who is speaking: some think they are the lovers themselves, others that they are the brothers or the companions. What is clear is that the vine represents the love of the couple, which is just beginning to flower, and the little foxes are threats that seem minor but can ruin everything.

For today: valuable relationships are harmed more by small neglects than by great crises. Think of one detail you are letting slide, such as a harsh word, a stored-up resentment, or lack of time together, and attend to it today with care and sincerity.
exp.5:4:
Here the beloved tells his bride to turn her eyes away from him, because they have overcome him, as if he had lost a battle. Then he compares her hair to a flock of goats coming down in a line over the hills of Gilead, a region of pasture. "Flock" means a group of animals being herded, and the image can be understood as the hair seen moving down the slope, like dark, shining waves.

The husband is speaking, in a love poem between two lovers. He has just praised her as majestic, and now he admits that her gaze has disarmed him. Many read this as poetic language of admiration; others also see an image of the love between God and his people, though that is debated.

For today: learn to express sincere and specific admiration to your spouse or to the person you love. A few words of appreciation, said with tenderness, strengthen affection and remind us that love is a gift that must be cared for.
exp.0:9:
He says that the beloved's cheeks look lovely adorned with jewels, and her neck looks beautiful with chains of gold. Jewels that hang near the face, like earrings, and chains of gold worn around the neck are the kind of ornaments he has in mind. It is a compliment to her beauty.

Here the beloved speaks, addressing the young woman. She has just voiced doubts about herself, and he reassures her with tender words. The verses that follow speak of making her more ornaments of gold and silver. Some understand the book as a poem about married love; others also see in it a picture of God's love for his people. Scholars do not fully agree on how it should be read.

For today: let us learn to speak sincere words of appreciation to those we love, especially when they feel insecure. A compliment given with affection can encourage them and strengthen the bond between you.
exp.5:6:
It says that the beloved's temples, that is, the part of the face beside the eyes and the forehead, look like a piece of a split pomegranate, and that they can be seen among her locks. "Locks" are the long strands of hair, and "pieces" here means slices or sections. The image probably speaks of a soft blush and a delicate color behind the veil or the hair, although some interpret it differently.

The lover speaks in this love poem and praises his beloved with images from the countryside, as he did in 4:3. His admiration is so great that he says her eyes have overcome him. Then he declares her unique among many women.

For today: learn to look with gratitude and to express in simple words what you value in your spouse or in the people you love. A sincere and specific compliment strengthens bonds and reflects the care God wants to see in our relationships.
exp.7:13:
It says the beloved should "flee," that is, make haste and come quickly, swift like a gazelle (a kind of deer) or a young stag. He runs upon the mountains of spices, places full of perfumes and fragrant plants. It is a final invitation full of tenderness and longing.

The one speaking is the beloved woman, the young woman of the poem. The book ends with her calling to her lover after speaking of her vineyard, which represents her life and her own care. Some understand that "flee" does not mean escape but coming with speed. Others read it as a longing left open. Many Christians also see in it a reflection of the Church's longing for Christ, though that reading is interpretive.

For today: express your longing to be close to God and to the people you love. Set aside time to pray simply and to nurture those relationships with constant affection.
exp.0:14:
In this verse, the beloved tells his beloved that she is beautiful, and he repeats it to add force. "My love" is an affectionate expression, like "my dear companion". What stands out most are her eyes, which he compares to a dove's, a symbol of tenderness, purity and simplicity.

Here the husband speaks, answering her words, since she has just praised him. Then she returns the praise: "you are handsome, my beloved". The book is poetry of love between two people. Some read it only as a celebration of married love; others also see a reflection of God's love for his people. Christians have held both readings.

For today: do not keep sincere praise to yourself. If you love someone, tell them in clear words what you value in that person. An honest compliment, spoken with affection, strengthens a marriage and any friendship as well.
exp.3:14:
She says the beloved is like a fountain that waters the gardens, and like a well of living water, that is, fresh water that keeps flowing and does not stand still. That water comes down from Lebanon, a region of high mountains, known for its snow and its clear streams.

Here the husband speaks in this love poem. He had been describing his beloved as a enclosed garden, full of fruit and fragrance. Now he emphasizes that this garden has abundant and pure water. Many understand it as an image of the beauty and life of married love; others also see a spiritual meaning, but the text does not state this clearly.

For today: care for your important relationships with words and gestures that give life, like fresh water. Value the people you love and do not let routine dry up the relationship.
exp.2:4:
She says she firmly asks the daughters of Jerusalem and makes them swear by the gazelles and the does of the field (delicate, graceful animals) not to awaken or disturb love until love itself is ready.

The word "I charge" means to ask solemnly, almost as an oath.

The bride, the Shulammite, has just searched for her beloved in the night, found him, and brought him into her mother's house. After that intense search, she warns her friends that love should not be forced or rushed. Some understand this as a call to wait for the right time; others as a call to guard the intimacy already experienced.

For today: do not force relationships or rush into love. Trust God, let everything mature in its own time, and take care of what is sacred.
exp.4:4:
She says that the woman finally got up to open the door for her beloved. Her hands and fingers were dripping with myrrh, a costly and strongly scented perfume, which ran down over the bolts, that is, the bars or latches of the door.

The woman who speaks in the poem is the beloved. Her lover had knocked at the door at night, and she hesitated out of comfort. When her heart was moved, she got up. There are several interpretations of the myrrh: it may be perfume she had put on herself, or perfume he had left behind. What we do see is that she responded, though late, as the next verse shows.

Today: when you feel the call of God or of someone who loves you, do not put it off for the sake of comfort. Respond promptly, because some opportunities do not wait.
exp.2:0:
She says that during the night she searched her bed for the one she loves with all her being, but did not find him. "Bed" is the place where she looked, and "I sought him" expresses the longing and the absence.

The beloved young woman of the Song of Songs speaks, in a love poem between her and her beloved. Many read it as a real scene, and others as a dream or an image of love's restlessness. There is no complete agreement. What follows shows that she gets up and goes out to look for him through the city, with sincere desire.

For today: when you feel that something is missing in a relationship, or even in your closeness to God, do not stop at complaining. Seek with steady effort, pray with honesty, and take concrete steps to draw nearer.
exp.0:4:
Here the young woman says she is dark-skinned, that is, her skin is dark and tanned. Although she says it with some shame, she affirms that she is "lovely," meaning beautiful and worthy of being loved. She compares herself to the dark tents of goat's hair of a nomadic tribe, and to the finest curtains, which suggest beauty and royal luxury.

The beloved speaks, addressing the daughters of Jerusalem, a group of women of the court. She feels watched and somewhat insecure about her sun-weathered skin, as she explains later: she worked in the vineyards. Her comparison joins the humble and the valuable. Some see here only human love; others read it also as an image of God's love for his people.

For today: do not let the opinions of others, or the marks of your work and life, define your worth. God sees you with love. Learn to accept yourself with honesty and gratitude, without hiding or comparing yourself to others.
exp.4:1:
She says she was asleep, but her heart was still alert. Then she hears the voice of her beloved knocking at the door. He calls her with affection: "my sister, my friend, my dove, my perfect one." He asks her to open to him because he is coming in wet: his head is full of dew, and his hair is soaked with the moisture of the night. "Open to me" is the phrase the verse uses for the knocking request.

The bride speaks, recalling a scene. Shortly before, the groom had said that he entered his garden, and that poetic language expresses the intimacy of marriage. Now he returns and knocks. Afterward she will hesitate: she had already gone to bed and did not want to get up. Some see here only human love; others also see an image of Christ and his people. Both readings have been held.

For today: when God or the people you love seek you, do not let comfort or tiredness make you indifferent. Keep your heart alert and respond promptly.
exp.2:5:
The passage asks who this woman is, coming up from the wilderness like a column of smoke. She is perfumed with myrrh and frankincense and with every kind of fine spice. "Perfumed with smoke" means scented with fragrant smoke, and "powders of the merchant" are perfumes or spices in powder form.

The one asking the question is not entirely clear. It could be the poet or a chorus, perhaps the daughters of Jerusalem. Then Solomon's litter with its escort appears, so many see here a wedding procession. Some think "this" refers to the bride, and others think it refers to the litter. The text allows both readings.

For today: true love deserves care, beauty and respect. In your daily dealings, cultivate a sweet fragrance: kind words, faithfulness and patience that speak well of your faith.
exp.5:1:
He says his beloved has gone down into his garden, to the beds of spices, to graze among the gardens and to gather lilies. "Beds of spices" refers to raised plots or rows where fragrant plants grow. "Graze" here means to feed or browse, and "gather" means to pick.

The bride is speaking, answering the women of Jerusalem, who had asked where her beloved has gone. She knows where to find him. Many read the garden and the lilies as poetic images of love and closeness between the two; others also see an allegory of God's love for his people, though the text does not say this directly.

For today: when you feel distance in an important relationship, do not stay in anguish. Remember what you know of that person and return to the place of meeting, with trust and affection. This also applies to your relationship with God.
exp.6:3:
She says her neck is like a tower of ivory, meaning elegant, slender, and precious. Her eyes are like the pools of Heshbon, an ancient city, beside the gate of Bath-rabbim; it is thought that this speaks of clear, deep, and calm eyes. Her nose is like the tower of Lebanon that looks toward Damascus, an image of strength and dignity, though today it may sound strange to us.

The one speaking is the bridegroom, who praises his beloved with images from his culture: towers, cities, and mountains. It is love poetry, not a literal description. Some see only marital love; others also see a reflection of God's love for his people.

Today we can learn to look at the person we love with appreciation and to say so with sincere and respectful words. A word of admiration can strengthen a marriage and show that we value the one God has given us.
exp.0:1:
What it says: The speaker strongly desires to receive signs of affection from her beloved. "Kisses" is an old word meaning kisses. She says that his love is better than wine, which at that time was a symbol of joy and celebration.

Context: The Song of Songs opens as a love song, attributed to Solomon. Here the young woman who is loved is speaking, and the "maidens" who appear later seem to be a chorus of companions. Interpreters understand it in several ways: as a poem about married love, or also as a picture of the love between God and his people. Many Christians accept both readings.

For today: God created human love as a good gift. If you are married, express affection to your spouse with simple words and gestures. And remember that the love of God gladdens the heart more than any passing pleasure.
exp.6:12:
Here the beloved says that the mandrakes already give off their fragrance, and that at the gate of her home she has all kinds of delicious fruits, fresh and kept from before. "Old" means from the previous harvest, and "sweet fruits" are exquisite fruits. She has set all of it aside for her beloved. Mandrakes were strong-smelling plants that in ancient times were associated with love, though scholars do not agree on all the details.

The young wife speaks in this love song. She has just invited her beloved to go out into the countryside, in spring, among the vineyards and pomegranate trees. Now she tells him that what she offers is abundant and prepared with care, both the new and the already known.

For today: faithful love is nurtured with generosity and thoughtful details. If you are married, look for a concrete way to surprise your spouse this week, and thank God for the good things he has already given you.
exp.3:10:
It says the bride's words are sweet and pleasing, like honey dripping from the honeycomb. "Honey and milk under your tongue" speaks of something sweet and nourishing. The fragrance of her garments is compared to that of Lebanon, a region known for its cedars and its fragrance. The idea of dripping means flowing slowly, drop by drop.

The one speaking is the bridegroom, who praises his beloved in this love poem. He has already said that she has captured his heart. Here he admires the way she speaks and her presence. Many see in the book a song of marital love; others also see a reflection of God's love for his people, though that is interpreted in several ways.

For today: use your words to bless. If you are married, today say a sincere word of affection and gratitude to your spouse. If not, do the same with someone close to you.
exp.4:15:
He says that the beloved's mouth is very sweet, and that all of him is desirable, worthy of being loved. "Palate" here refers to the mouth or to speech; "desirable" means wanted and admired, not in the sense of wrongful greed.
