The bride ends her description by saying, "This is my beloved, and this is my friend," and she addresses the daughters of Jerusalem.

The speaker is the bride, the beloved of the book. The women of Jerusalem had asked her what is so special about her beloved (5:9). She answers by describing him from head to foot with images of gold, ivory, and cedar. Many see here marital love; others, following a traditional reading, also see a reflection of the love between God and his people. How to combine these two readings is debated.

For today: learn to speak appreciation out loud for those you love. If you are married, speak well of your spouse and thank them for the good you see in that person. And in your faith, ask yourself whether you could say of Christ: "This is my beloved, and this is my friend."
exp.4:13:
The bride says that her beloved's hands are like gold rings set with precious stones (the words "set with" describe stones placed into the rings). The "beryl" was a precious stone of an intense color, though it is not known with certainty which stone it was. His "belly", that is, his torso, is like bright ivory adorned with sapphires, which were perhaps blue like lapis lazuli.

The bride is speaking. The daughters of Jerusalem had asked her what makes her beloved special, and she answers with a portrait full of images of riches, strength and beauty. These are poetic metaphors, not a literal description.

For today: learn to value and to express in concrete words the good qualities of the people you love. Today, tell your spouse, a family member or a friend something specific that you admire in him or her.
exp.0:6:
The woman asks her beloved to tell her where he feeds his flock and where he makes them rest at noon, when the heat is strong. "Feeding" means leading to pasture, and "resting place" is the place where the sheep lie down. She does not want to wander aimlessly among the flocks of other shepherds.

The young woman of the book speaks, addressing her beloved, whom she imagines as a shepherd. She comes from feeling insecure because of her sun-darkened skin and the hard work her brothers imposed on her. Now she seeks to be with the one she loves. Some see here a poem of human love; others, an image of the love between God and his people, or between Christ and the Church.

For today: when you feel tired or without direction, seek God in prayer and in his Word, and ask him to guide you and give you rest.
exp.5:12:
It says that someone calls the Shulamite to return, and repeats the call four times because they want to look at her. Then it asks, "What will ye see in the Shulamite?" and answers, "As it were the company of two armies." The word "return" means "turn back" or "come back." "Shulamite" seems to be a name or title for the beloved. The phrase about the two armies can also be translated as "the dance of Mahanaim," and scholars interpret it in several ways: a dance, a camp of angels, or a place with two groups.

A chorus, perhaps the women of Jerusalem, is asking the beloved to come back. Then she or the beloved responds with a question. The exact meaning is not certain. It comes after she says that her soul made her tremble like the chariots of Amminadab.

For today: God looks upon us with honor, not with mockery. But we can also learn to receive the gaze of others with humility and without shame, remembering that our identity rests in the love of God.
exp.4:14:
He says the beloved's legs are firm like pillars of marble, set upon bases of pure gold. The bases are the pedestals that the pillars stand on. His appearance, or his bearing, is majestic like Mount Lebanon, famous for its cedars, which were tall, strong, and very valuable trees.

The speaker is the bride, the Shulammite. The women of Jerusalem have asked her what makes her beloved so special, and she describes him from head to toe with poetic images. Many believe this speaks of marital love; some Christians also see a reflection of Christ's love for his people, though this is an interpretive reading.

For today: learn to admire the people you love with sincere words. And if you follow Christ, set aside time to contemplate his strength and his faithfulness, so that your love for him may grow.
exp.1:1:
Here the lover speaks and says that his beloved, in today's language his sweetheart, stands out among the other young women like a lily among thorns. The young women are unmarried girls. The thorns are not an insult to the others but a contrast to show how brightly she shines in his eyes.

It is a dialogue of love poetry. The woman has just described herself with humility as a common flower. He answers by raising her worth. Then she will reply by praising him as an apple tree among the wild trees. Some see here only romantic love between a couple; others also see an image of God's love for his people. Both readings have been held.

For today: let us learn to say words that encourage and affirm those we love, especially those who feel small. A sincere expression of appreciation can give someone courage and security.
exp.5:0:
Here, some friends, called "the daughters of Jerusalem," ask the bride where her beloved has gone. They call her "the fairest among women," and they offer to seek him with her. The words "gone" and "turned aside" mean that he went to another place. "That we may seek him" means "that we may seek him" with her.

The chorus of women speaks here, after she described her beloved with such tenderness at the end of chapter 5. Her praise has aroused their curiosity. She will answer that he is in his garden. Many read this as poetry of marital love; others also see an image of the love between God and his people. Interpreters understand it in different ways.

For today: when we speak with joy about what we love, others become interested. Let us speak sincerely about Christ and what He does in our lives, and let us accompany those who seek Him.
exp.4:7:
Here the young woman speaks to the daughters of Jerusalem, and she urges them earnestly: if they find her beloved, they should tell him that she is sick with love, that is, weak and wounded by longing to see him.

She is the bride of the book. She has just gone looking for her beloved at night; he was not there, and the city watchmen struck her and took away her cloak. Hurt and distressed, she asks other women for help. Interpreters read this in different ways: as a dream, as a real event, or as a poem about human love. Many Christians also see in it a reflection of the love between Christ and his people.

For today: when you feel distance or pain, do not keep it silent or carry it alone. Ask trusted brothers and sisters to pray with you, and keep seeking God with sincerity.
exp.3:6:
He says that the bridegroom looks at his beloved and sees her as wholly beautiful. He calls her with an affectionate phrase, and he speaks of a blemish, meaning a defect or imperfection. He sees nothing in her that takes away from her worth in his eyes.

In this poem, the speaker is the beloved, addressing the bride. He has just described her beauty with poetic images, and this line sums up his praise. Many read it as a song of marital love; others also see in it an image of God's love for his people. Christians have interpreted the book in both ways.

For today: if you are married, practice looking at your partner and saying what is good in them, without dwelling only on their faults. And if you feel of little worth, remember that God loves you with tenderness, and your worth does not depend on being perfect.
exp.4:6:
The woman tells how, while she was wandering through the city looking for her beloved, the night watchmen found her. They struck her, hurt her, and took away her cloak, the garment she used to cover herself. The verse says they "wounded" her, and the watchmen are the guards who patrol the city.

The young wife is the speaker of the poem. Her beloved came, but she was slow to open the door, and he left. Now she searches for him in anguish and cannot find him. She suffers unfair treatment in her search. Many readers understand this scene as a dream or a poetic image of the pain of a wounded love; others see it as a real event within the story. The text does not make this clear.

For today: when a relationship grows cold through carelessness or delay, do not let it slide. Act in time, seek reconciliation with humility and love. And in your life with God, respond promptly when He calls you, without putting it off.
exp.2:3:
Here the woman tells how, just a little after she had passed the city's watchmen, she found the one her soul loves. She took hold of him firmly, would not let him go, and brought him into her mother's house, into the room where she was conceived and born.

The young woman who speaks is the beloved in the Song of Songs, a love poem between her and her lover. Earlier she searched for him through the streets at night and did not find him, and she grew anxious. Then the meeting brings her relief and joy. Bringing him to her mother's house suggests a desire for a lasting union blessed by the family. Some readers also see a reflection of the love between God and his people, though this is understood in various ways.

For today: when you seek God or care for an important relationship, do not give up in the waiting. Persevere, and when you find what is precious, hold on to it with gratitude and commitment.
exp.3:7:
Here the bridegroom calls his beloved to come with him from Lebanon. He asks her to look down from the peaks of Amana, Senir and Hermon, which are mountains in the north of Israel. He mentions the lions' dens and the mountains of the leopards, which probably refers to leopards, wild and dangerous places. "Spouse" here is a term of affection and commitment.

The bridegroom speaks in the Song of Songs, a love poem. He has just praised her for her beauty, and now he invites her to go out with him. Some see in the dangerous mountains a place of fear or distance, and in his call a desire to draw her close to himself. Others see it only as poetic imagery. The exact meaning is not known with certainty.

For today: when love invites you to move forward, do not let fear hold you back. In marriage and in faith, walking together with confidence overcomes places that seem dangerous.
exp.7:7:
They speak of a younger sister who is still young and has not yet matured physically. They ask what they will do for her on the day when she is spoken for, that is, when the time comes for someone to ask for her hand in marriage. It is a question of family care and protection.

Those who speak seem to be the beloved's brothers, though the text does not say so with complete clarity. Then the young woman answers that she is already a wall and has found peace beside her beloved. Some understand that the brothers are speaking of a younger sister; others, that they are speaking of the beloved herself when she was a child. Both readings are possible.

For today: caring for those who are young and vulnerable is a task of love and wisdom. We can accompany them with prayer, good example and counsel, without controlling them, so that they mature with strength and learn to decide well.
exp.6:6:
It says the beloved's figure is tall and slender like a palm tree, and that her breasts are like clusters of dates or grapes. "Stature" is her height or bearing, and the comparison describes her as like the palm. It is poetic language praising her beauty.

Here the beloved, the husband, speaks in a love song between two people. He admires his wife from head to foot and uses images from nature. In the verse that follows, he speaks of wanting to climb the palm tree, that is, he expresses his desire and affection for her. Interpreters read this as poetry of marital love; some also see in it a reflection of God's love for his people, though this is debated.

For today: if you are married, encourage your spouse with sincere and respectful words of appreciation. The Bible presents married love as something good and worth celebrating, marked by faithfulness and tenderness.
exp.7:11:
She says that the woman looks after her own vineyard, that is, herself and her life, and that she decides to whom she gives it. Solomon is owed the thousand pieces of silver, and two hundred go to those who take care of the fruit. "Keep" means look after or watch over. "Before me" shows that it is under her own care.

The beloved young woman of the Song is speaking. Earlier she set Solomon's vineyard, which brought in a great deal and was entrusted to keepers, against her own, which is not for sale. Many understand the vineyard to stand for her person and her love, though others read it in a simpler way. Her answer is that her giving is free and cannot be bought with riches.

For today: value your life and your affections as a gift that God has entrusted to you. Look after them with wisdom, and do not trade them for money, pressure or convenience, but give them freely and faithfully.
exp.3:1:
Your teeth are like a flock of sheep freshly sheared, coming up clean from the washing place. All of them bear twins, and none has lost her lambs. That is, white, even, and complete teeth, with none missing. "Barren" here means without young, and "twins" refers to pairs, which suggests symmetry.

The one speaking is the bridegroom, who praises his beloved in a love poem. He describes her face with images from the countryside, very common for his time. Scholars agree that this is poetic language, not a literal description. Some also see a reflection of God's love for his people, though this is interpreted in several ways.

For today: learn to praise the people you love with sincere and specific words. A thoughtful and affectionate compliment, especially in marriage, strengthens the bond and makes the other person feel valued.
exp.6:11:
Here the bride invites her beloved to get up early and go out to the vineyards. She wants to see whether the vines have budded, whether the blossoms are opening, and whether the pomegranates have flowered. There she tells him she will give him her love, that is, her affection and her devotion.

The bride speaks in the Song of Songs, a poem about love between a man and a woman. She has just declared that she belongs to her beloved, and now she proposes that they go out together into the countryside, away from everyday life. Some read it only as marital love; others also see a reflection of God's love for his people. Both readings have been held throughout history.

For today: love is cared for with intentional time. Set aside a moment, without rush or screens, to be with your spouse, or with the Lord, and see how what you have planted grows.
exp.1:4:
Here the young woman asks to be strengthened with raisin cakes and apples. Her wording, in the older translation, uses a word for these raisin cakes, and when she asks to be sustained she is asking for strength. She says she is sick with love, meaning she is so full of emotion for her beloved that she feels weak and overwhelmed.

The one speaking is the bride, the young woman of the poem. She has just described her beloved as a sweet and protecting apple tree, and recalled that he brought her into the banqueting house, a place of feasting, where his banner over her was love, meaning his sign over her was affection. She is overcome with the joy of being loved.

For today: true love is a beautiful gift, but it needs care. Ask God for wisdom to love with tenderness and without haste.
exp.0:5:
She says she does not want to be looked down on because of her dark skin. The sun burned her. Her brothers grew angry with her and put her to work keeping other people's vineyards, so she could not look after her own vineyard. "Grew angry" is the meaning of the verb here. The word for her skin describes skin darkened by the sun.

The young woman of the book, the beloved, speaks here to the daughters of Jerusalem. She has just said she is dark but beautiful. Now she explains why: she worked hard out in the open air because her family ordered her to. Her "vineyard" may mean her own person or her own life; interpreters understand it in several ways.

God does not see as people see. If others judge you by your appearance, your background, or the burdens of your past, remember that your worth does not depend on those things. Rest in the love of God and take wise care of your own life.
exp.4:11:
His eyes are like doves beside streams of water, bathed in milk, and set just right. This verse describes the beloved's eyes with images of beauty and tenderness. They are like doves beside streams of water, which seem bathed in milk, that is, clean and bright. The phrase "set just right" means they are placed perfectly, like a jewel in its setting. Some scholars understand the expression to refer to the eyes, and others to the doves.

In this passage the wife is speaking. The women of Jerusalem ask her what is so special about her beloved, and she answers with a description from head to toe. She does so in poetic, not literal, language. Many Christians also see here a reflection of the love between Christ and his people, although this is interpreted in different ways.

For today: let us learn to look at the people we love with admiration and gratitude, and to tell them what we value in them. Sincere words of appreciation strengthen affection and trust in the family and among friends.
exp.5:10:
It tells of someone who went down to a garden of walnut trees to look at the fruits of the valley. They wanted to see whether the vines were already putting out new shoots and whether the pomegranates were already in bloom. The second word for "to" is an older form of the same preposition, and "to bud" means beginning to send out new growth.

The speaker is the beloved, or according to other readings the beloved woman, in this love poem. Interpreters do not fully agree on who is speaking. It comes right after the lover has praised her beauty. Here the garden seems to be a poetic image of intimacy and of love that is beginning to flourish. In the next verse, the emotion unsettles and surprises him.

For today: love, like a garden, calls for attention and constant visits. Set aside time to look with affection at how your marriage, your family and your faith are doing, and patiently tend what is just beginning to bud.
exp.3:8:
He says the bridegroom is completely captivated by his beloved. "You have ravished my heart" means that she has stolen his heart, or made him fall in love. She accomplished this with just one glance ("one of your eyes") and with a piece of jewelry from her neck, a delicate necklace or ornament. Calling her "sister" does not indicate kinship; it was an affectionate expression of closeness and tenderness.

The bridegroom speaks in this love poem. He has just praised her beauty and invites her to come with him from the northern mountains. Many understand this as an invitation to leave dangerous or distant places. Some see here only love between spouses; others also see a reflection of God's love for his people. Interpreters explain it in several ways.

For today: learn to admire and to express, in simple words, what you value in your spouse or in the people you love. A small gesture, a glance, or a kind phrase can strengthen a relationship.
exp.6:7:
Here the husband says that he decided to climb the palm tree and take hold of its branches, that is, to draw close to his beloved with affection.

He compares her breasts to clusters of grapes and the scent of her breath to that of apples. Some scholars believe that this fruit could be something else, such as the apricot, but the idea is one of sweetness and freshness.

The one speaking is the husband, who praises his wife with images from nature. The book celebrates married love, using poetic and very intimate language. In the next verse she takes up the word and answers that she belongs to her beloved.

For today: the Bible presents love between spouses as a good gift from God. If you are married, express your affection to your spouse with tender and sincere words, and care for that intimacy with faithfulness and respect.
exp.1:12:
This verse describes spring: the fig tree already has its first fruit, and the vines in blossom fill the air with fragrance. The phrase "in bloom" here means they are flowering, about to bear fruit. With that picture, the beloved invites his lover: "Arise, my love, my fair one, and come away."

The husband speaks in this love poem from the Song of Songs. Winter and the rain have already passed, and he calls his beloved tenderly, as she seems to be withdrawn in a hidden place. Many Christians see in this also an image of God's love for his people, though others read it only as poetry about human love.

For today: if you are going through a difficult season, do not remain shut inside it. God is patient and invites you to come out with hope. Notice the small signs of renewal around you.
exp.3:9:
It says the beloved's love is beautiful and much better than wine. Her fragrance is worth more than all the aromatic spices. The lover's word for affection here refers to caresses or expressions of tenderness. The affectionate way he addresses her is a word of closeness, not a claim about family relationship. The fragrant oils were perfumes or aromatic oils.

The one speaking is the beloved, the bridegroom, addressing his wife in the Song of Songs. He has just said that she stole his heart with a single glance. It is a poem of married love, full of sensual imagery. Some read it also as a reflection of God's love for his people, and others read it only as a celebration of human love. Both readings have been held throughout history.

For today: do not keep your words of appreciation to yourself. If you are married, or caring for someone with affection, tell that person today, sincerely, what you value in them. Love grows stronger when it is expressed with tenderness and gratitude.

sum.1: In this chapter, the young woman and her beloved praise each other tenderly. She compares him to an apple tree that gives shade and sweet fruit, and he sees her as a lily among thorns. He invites her to come out with him because spring has arrived, and she declares, "My beloved is mine, and I am his." She also asks that love be guarded and not rushed.
sum.4: In this chapter, the bridegroom arrives at his garden, and the beloved, hesitating to open the door, loses him. She goes out to search for him, but the watchmen wound her. Then she asks the young women for help and lovingly describes how beautiful and precious her beloved is. The passage shows a deep love, one that sometimes faces delay and pain.
sum.2: At night, the beloved searches for her lover. She does not find him, so she goes through the city until she finds him and brings him to her mother's house. She asks the women of Jerusalem not to stir up love before its time. Then Solomon's sedan chair appears, surrounded by guards, and people are invited to come and see the king wearing the crown on his wedding day.
sum.7: In this final chapter, the beloved wishes she could love her lover openly and without shame, and she says that true love is as strong as death, and that neither rivers nor riches can put it out or buy it. She also speaks of her little sister and of Solomon's vineyard, and she ends by inviting her beloved to come quickly. Interpreters explain verses 8 to 12 in several different ways.
sum.5: The women of Jerusalem ask where the beloved has gone, and the beloved replies that he is in his garden and that the two of them belong to each other. The lover praises her beauty and says she is unique, the perfect one, and that queens and young women all call her blessed. At the end, she tells how she went down to the garden and was overcome with emotion, and they ask her to come back. The text is poetic and somewhat hard to understand.
sum.3: In this chapter the bridegroom praises the beauty of his beloved with poetic images, from her eyes down to her neck, and invites her to come with him, saying that she has captivated his heart. He calls her a "garden enclosed" and a "sealed fountain," words that many understand to express purity and exclusivity. She replies by inviting her beloved to come into her garden.
sum.0: In this chapter, a young woman and her beloved express a deep love full of admiration for each other. She describes herself as dark-skinned and says she worked looking after other people's vineyards, while she longs to be close to him. The two praise each other with images of perfume, flowers, and a dove. Many also read it as a teaching about the value of faithful love.
sum.6: In this chapter, the husband praises the beauty of his beloved with poetic images, from her feet to her head, and expresses his desire for her. She responds that she belongs to her beloved and invites him to go out into the countryside, to the vineyards, to give her love to him. The book celebrates married love, its tenderness and its joy.
